nameStory: The Atlantic dogwhelk gets its unusual name from its reputation as a fierce predator of the rocky shores - like a dog that won't let go of its prey. The "whelk" part comes from the Old English word for a spiral shell, while "dog" refers to its tenacious hunting behavior as it drills into other shellfish.
description: The Atlantic dogwhelk is a chunky, spiral-shelled sea snail that's one of the rocky coast's most successful predators. These carnivorous marine snails typically grow about 1-2 inches tall, with thick, sturdy shells that can handle the pounding waves of New England's shores. Their shells range from white to yellow, brown, or even purple, often with darker banding patterns. You'll find them crawling over rocks and barnacles, hunting for their next meal.

idTips.label: Thick, robust shell
idTips.description: The shell feels heavy and solid in your hand, with thick walls that can withstand crashing waves - much sturdier than typical garden snails

idTips.label: Pointed spire with whorls
idTips.description: The shell spirals to a sharp point with 6-7 distinct whorls that you can count by running your finger along the shell's surface

idTips.label: Wide opening (aperture)
idTips.description: The shell opening is large and oval-shaped, taking up about half the shell's height, with a smooth rim that feels polished

idTips.label: Variable colors
idTips.description: Shells can be bright white, creamy yellow, rich brown, or deep purple, sometimes with dark spiral bands you can trace with your fingertip

idTips.label: Rough texture
idTips.description: The shell surface often feels slightly bumpy or ridged rather than perfectly smooth, with growth lines that catch your fingernail

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: About the size of your thumb tip, with a cone-like shape that's wider at the base than most spiral shells

habitat: Atlantic dogwhelks thrive on rocky shores throughout New England's coastline, from Maine to Connecticut. Look for them in the intertidal zone - the area between high and low tides - where they cling to rocks, pier pilings, and jetties. They're especially common around mussel beds and barnacle colonies, which serve as their primary hunting grounds.

seasonality.spring: Active hunting season begins as water temperatures rise. You'll see them moving across rocks during low tides, often with their muscular foot extended.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when dogwhelks are most visible and mobile. This is the best time to observe their predatory behavior and see fresh, clean shells.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to slow down. Shells may show more wear from summer activities, and you might find egg cases attached to rocks.
seasonality.winter: Least active period, often hiding in crevices or under seaweed. Empty shells are more commonly found washed up on beaches after winter storms.

funFact: Atlantic dogwhelks are shell-drilling assassins - they use their rasping tongue (called a radula) to bore perfectly round holes through the shells of mussels and barnacles, then inject digestive enzymes to liquify their prey and slurp out the contents like a gruesome smoothie!
confusionNotes: Dogwhelks are most often confused with periwinkles, but dogwhelks have much thicker, more robust shells and pointed spires, while periwinkles are smaller with more rounded, dome-like shells. Remember: dogwhelks are chunky and cone-shaped, periwinkles are petite and globe-shaped.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "whelk," the Atlantic dogwhelk isn't closely related to true whelks like the knobbed whelk. It's actually in the murex family, known as rock snails. This naming confusion is common with marine mollusks, where "whelk" has become a catch-all term for many spiral-shelled sea snails.
compareHints: Since the Atlantic dogwhelk is the only Nucella species in New England waters, compare it to other murex family members like the oyster drill. Dogwhelks are generally larger and more robust than oyster drills, with less pronounced ridges or spines on their shells. Unlike the more ornate shells of some murex relatives, dogwhelks have a relatively simple, streamlined design built for life in the rough intertidal zone.
